stories.headline: 5.3 magnitude earthquake strikes Nepal, tremors felt across five countries
stories.title: 5.3 magnitude earthquake strikes Nepal, tremors felt across five countries
stories.summary: Srinagar, Nov 24: A magnitude 5.4 earthquake struck near Lelep in Nepal’s Koshi Province at around 7:02 am on Tuesday, sending tremors across parts of India, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh and China. According to the National Centre for Seismology (NCS), the earthquake originated at a depth of 20 kilometres, with its epicentre at 27.855° N latitude and 87.909° E longitude. In India, tremors were felt in Jalpaiguri district of West Bengal, triggering panic among residents, who rushed out of their homes. No casualties or damage to property have been reported so far.

stories.title: India warns Ukraine war food disruption could mirror Bengal famine’s impact on Global South
stories.summary: India told the UN Security Council that the Ukraine war's disruption of global food supplies could have devastating consequences for the Global South, drawing parallels with the 1943 Bengal famine. India called for protecting Black Sea food supply routes, civilian infrastructure and humanitarian access to prevent worsening food, fuel and fertiliser crises.

stories.headline: What oil's new plot twist means for India
stories.title: What oil's new plot twist means for India
stories.summary: The fear of a renewal of war is again roiling the waters of Hormuz following Iran's warning that it will use "all available means" to break US's blockade. As the possibility of another bout of costly fighting looms, policymakers have begun looking anxiously at the geopolitical powder keg once more.Despite this big new threat to one of the world's most critical shipping corridors, oil prices moved in the opposite direction, falling below $90. The fall came on expectations of abundant global supplies offsetting the risk of another war, Reuters reported on November 24.Also read | Petrol, diesel prices rose 7% in India vs 50-70% globally over four years: Hardeep PuriAs oil markets shrug of the risk, for India it means relief at a time when risks to its oil math and exports were seen to be building up again.With the unexpected, steady easing of crude prices amid worsening rhetoric coming as as a surprise, policymakers, oil refiners, shipping companies and exporters are trying to make sense of what it means for India.Why oil markets looked other wayAs of November 24, Brent delined 0.7% to $88.71 a barrel, while US WTI crude fell 0.8% to $79.57, with both benchmarks approaching three-month lows.Improving supply conditions were the reason why oil markets chose to look the other way, Reuters reported. Libya's reopening of its Sharara pipeline has restored additional flows even as global inventories begin to rebuild.According to a Deutsche Bank estimate, global liquid fuel inventories rose substantially in October -- by 52 million barrels, which means a surplus of around 1.7 million barrels a day.Oil markets are seemingly betting that extra supplies can absorb more tensions on the Iran front, if any, various reports said citing industry analysts.The math may change quickly, though.Iran has positioned more than 14 tankers near Kharg Island, satellite imagery and shipping data showed. This indicated that preparations may be under way for possible shipping via Hormuz. If Iran's oil convoy ventures out, it will be running into the US blockade that is in place there. That will mean a costly, likely bloody face-off.Short-lived relief?For India, the fall in crude always brings good news. Lower oil prices brings down its import bill, reduces pressure on the rupee and helps keep inflation in check. A cheaper oil means major relief for India's oil industry -- retailers, refiners and businesses that rely on petro raw material.Also read | Govt tightens rules for oil, gas block extensions, seeks bigger profit shareBut a point to note here is that Hormuz means more for India than just crude. It is also the LNG lifeline for the country. Apart from 40-50% of India's crude imports, about 50-60% of India's LNG shipments also pass through the strait, ET reported recently citing Crisil's estimates.India imports approximately 85% of its crude requirements and half of its natural gas requirements. While crude chaos can disrupt transportation, a cut in the supply of natural gas will stop critical industries like fertilisers and chemicals in their track.If Iran tries to break through the blockade and the US responds with an attack, oil prices may then rise much faster than they have fallen. That is the big danger as of now.If a face-off occurs, a sudden $20-30 increase from the current levels cannot be ruled out, Reuters reported.Such a jump will take Brent towards $110-120, sharply erasing the price relief. If the fighting gets prolonged, that would mean a renewed competition for oil supplies, which will make freight and insurance costs soar.Crude cheaper, but there's more to itLower spot prices do not necessarily mean cheaper crude at Indian ports. This is because other problems like shipping costs, insurance premiums and delivery delays can majorly increase the final bill.Hindustan Petroleum, for instance, has flagged difficulties in booking tankers for Hormuz crossings, even as more vessels have resumed using the route, Bloomberg reported in early November.Indian refiners are already adjusting their buying strategies to account for this uncertainty.For example, Mangalore Refinery and Petrochemicals told Reuters that it now prefers to buy crude that is delivered to the port. This leaves transportation and associated risks with suppliers.Some of the Indian companies are also diversifying their supplies and looking at deliveries from outside the Gulf. Saudi Arabia's increased use of its Red Sea export terminal at Yanbu has provided an alternative route for some shipments.Not just oilIndia's Hormuz-related risks are not just about oil. It has substantial exports dealings across the Gulf, including basmati rice, pharmaceuticals, engineering goods, gems and jewellery. The UAE and Saudi Arabia are key destinations and distribution centres for Indian merchandise.For Indian exporters, another interruption could mean higher freight charges, delayed deliveries, higher insurance premiums and difficulties in collecting payments.Basmati exporters have faced uncertainty over shipments and payment channels, while pharmaceutical and livestock exporters have reported transportation and insurance worries, ET Small Biz reported a while ago.As a result, shipping companies and insurers are having to factor in the possibility of another sudden escalation.A few months ago, Indian insurers reviewed their exposure to Gulf-bound cargo and introduced additional war-risk premiums. ICICI Lombard, for instance, had introduced a war-risk premium of around 0.25% for Gulf-linked cargo in March, ET reported.Exporters, meanwhile, have an incentive to incorporate exceptional freight and insurance costs into contracts rather than absorb the entire increase themselves.If ships again have to avoid Hormuz, container lines will have to look at alternative routes. Sohar in Oman has emerged as an alternative gateway, with feeder services between India and the port increasing nearly fourfold during the Iran disruption, The Times of India reported in September.Indian exporters in double bindThe immediate danger is not just that oil prices may rise. It is that a face-off may simultaneously throw crude supplies, LNG deliveries and shipping out of gear.If a face-off occurs, tankers might refuse to enter the Gulf, insurers could reassess or withdraw coverage, and container operators could suspend services or divert ships, causing severe problems for Indian exportersEven those exports that are not directly exposed to Hormuz could face higher transportation costs as ships and containers become less available.Such a situation will likely bring back two worries -- a) a higher crude bill and b) more expensive exports. That will mean a double jeopardy for Indian exporters. Smaller exporters, which have limited bargaining power to pass on additional costs, may end up getting particularly badly hit.

opening: The fear of a renewal of war is again roiling the waters of Hormuz following Iran's warning that it will use "all available means" to break US's blockade.
As the possibility of another bout of costly fighting looms, policymakers have begun looking anxiously at the geopolitical powder keg once more.
body: Despite this big new threat to one of the world's most critical shipping corridors, oil prices moved in the opposite direction, falling below $90.
The fall came on expectations of abundant global supplies offsetting the risk of another war, Reuters reported on November 24.

Also read | Petrol, diesel prices rose 7% in India vs 50-70% globally over four years: Hardeep PuriAs oil markets shrug of the risk, for India it means relief at a time when risks to its oil math and exports were seen to be building up again.

With the unexpected, steady easing of crude prices amid worsening rhetoric coming as a surprise, policymakers, oil refiners, shipping companies and exporters are trying to make sense of what it means for India.
Why oil markets looked other wayAs of November 24, Brent delined 0.7% to $88.71 a barrel, while US WTI crude fell 0.8% to $79.57, with both benchmarks approaching three-month lows.
Improving supply conditions were the reason why oil markets chose to look the other way, Reuters reported.
Libya's reopening of its Sharara pipeline has restored additional flows even as global inventories begin to rebuild.
According to a Deutsche Bank estimate, global liquid fuel inventories rose substantially in October -- by 52 million barrels, which means a surplus of around 1.7 million barrels a day.
Oil markets are seemingly betting that extra supplies can absorb more tensions on the Iran front, if any, various reports said citing industry analysts.
The math may change quickly, though.
Iran has positioned more than 14 tankers near Kharg Island, satellite imagery and shipping data showed.
This indicated that preparations may be under way for possible shipping via Hormuz.
If Iran's oil convoy ventures out, it will be running into the US blockade that is in place there.
That will mean a costly, likely bloody face-off.
Short-lived relief?
For India, the fall in crude always brings good news.
Lower oil prices brings down its import bill, reduces pressure on the rupee and helps keep inflation in check.
A cheaper oil means major relief for India's oil industry -- retailers, refiners and businesses that rely on petro raw material.
Also read | Govt tightens rules for oil, gas block extensions, seeks bigger profit share.
But a point to note here is that Hormuz means more for India than just crude.
It is also the LNG lifeline for the country.
Apart from 40-50% of India's crude imports, about 50-60% of India's LNG shipments also pass through the strait, ET reported recently citing Crisil's estimates.
While crude chaos can disrupt transportation, a cut in the supply of natural gas will stop critical industries like fertilisers and chemicals in their track.
If Iran tries to break through the blockade and the US responds with an attack, oil prices may then rise much faster than they have fallen.
That is the big danger as of now.
If a face-off occurs, a sudden $20-30 increase from the current levels cannot be ruled out, Reuters reported.
Such a jump will take Brent towards $110-120, sharply erasing the price relief.
If the fighting gets prolonged, that would mean a renewed competition for oil supplies, which will make freight and insurance costs soar.
Crude cheaper, but there's more to itLower spot prices do not necessarily mean cheaper crude at Indian ports.
This is because other problems like shipping costs, insurance premiums and delivery delays can majorly increase the final bill.
Hindustan Petroleum, for instance, has flagged difficulties in booking tankers for Hormuz crossings, even as more vessels have resumed using the route, Bloomberg reported in early November.
Indian refiners are already adjusting their buying strategies to account for this uncertainty.
For example, Mangalore Refinery and Petrochemicals told Reuters that it now prefers to buy crude that is delivered to the port.
This leaves transportation and associated risks with suppliers.
Some of the Indian companies are also diversifying their supplies and looking at deliveries from outside the Gulf.
Saudi Arabia's increased use of its Red Sea export terminal at Yanbu has provided an alternative route for some shipments.
Not just oil.
India's Hormuz-related risks are not just about oil.
It has substantial exports dealings across the Gulf, including basmati rice, pharmaceuticals, engineering goods, gems and jewellery.
The UAE and Saudi Arabia are key destinations and distribution centres for Indian merchandise.
For Indian exporters, another interruption could mean higher freight charges, delayed deliveries, higher insurance premiums and difficulties in collecting payments.

Basmati exporters have faced uncertainty over shipments and payment channels, while pharmaceutical and livestock exporters have reported transportation and insurance worries, ET Small Biz reported a while ago.
As a result, shipping companies and insurers are having to factor in the possibility of another sudden escalation.
A few months ago, Indian insurers reviewed their exposure to Gulf-bound cargo and introduced additional war-risk premiums.
ICICI Lombard, for instance, had introduced a war-risk premium of around 0.25% for Gulf-linked cargo in March, ET reported.
Exporters, meanwhile, have an incentive to incorporate exceptional freight and insurance costs into contracts rather than absorb the entire increase themselves.
If ships again have to avoid Hormuz, container lines will have to look at alternative routes.
Sohar in Oman has emerged as an alternative gateway, with feeder services between India and the port increasing nearly fourfold during the Iran disruption, The Times of India reported in September.
Indian exporters in double bind.
The immediate danger is not just that oil prices may rise.
It is that a face-off may simultaneously throw crude supplies, LNG deliveries and shipping out of gear.

If a face-off occurs, tankers might refuse to enter the Gulf, insurers could reassess or withdraw coverage, and container operators could suspend services or divert ships, causing severe problems for Indian exportersEven those exports that are not directly exposed to Hormuz could face higher transportation costs as ships and containers become less available.
Such a situation will likely bring back two worries -- a) a higher crude bill and b) more expensive exports.
That will mean a double jeopardy for Indian exporters.
Smaller exporters, which have limited bargaining power to pass on additional costs, may end up getting particularly badly hit.

stories.headline: Ousted leader Hasina plans to return to Bangladesh from exile on Dec 16, spokesperson says
stories.title: Ousted leader Hasina plans to return to Bangladesh from exile on Dec 16, spokesperson says
stories.summary: Dhaka, Nov 24: Ousted Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina plans to return home from exile in India on December 16, the day the country celebrates as Victory Day when it won independence after a war with Pakistan. Hasina went into exile in India on August 5, 2024, after a student-led mass uprising forced her to end her 15-year rule. She was sentenced to death in absentia for crimes against humanity involving the uprising in which hundreds of protesters were killed. Hasina rejected the verdict and has said she is ready fight the case once she is back. In the statement Tuesday announcing the planned date of her return, she urged current Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to arrange her return on the national airline. “Since Sheikh Hasina was flown to India on a Bangladesh aircraft on August 5th, 2024, she now calls upon the government to arrange for her air transport from Delhi back to Dhaka,” spokesman Syed Mozammel Ali said in the statement. “It is deeply symbolic that she has chosen 16 December, our Victory Day, for her planned return to Bangladesh. We firmly believe that she will celebrate this historic day among her people, honouring the great victory achieved under the leadership of her father, Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman," Abu Obaidha Arin, an aide to Hasina, told The Associated Press. “We are equally confident that, she will definitely return and under her leadership post return, Bangladesh will once again advance towards peace, stability and prosperity,” Arin said. Earlier this month, in an interview with The Associated Press, Hasina said she would return to the country in December at any cost, and even death could not prevent her from returning home.

stories.headline: Supreme Court Stays Kerala High Court Judgment Allowing Restructuring Of Police Associations And Abolition Of KPOA
stories.title: Supreme Court Stays Kerala High Court Judgment Allowing Restructuring Of Police Associations And Abolition Of KPOA
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Supreme Court has stayed a Kerala High Court judgment which had upheld the State government's decision to restructure recognised police associations in Kerala by abolishing the Kerala.
Police Officers' Association (KPOA) and redistributing its members between two other associations.

A bench of Justice BV Nagarathna and Justice Sanjeev Sachdeva put on hold the Division Bench ruling of November 12, 2026, which had set aside a Single Judge decision quashing the government's restructuring order dated July 27, 2026.
The dispute concerns a government order reorganising the three recognised police associations in the State – the Kerala.
Police Association (KPA), the Kerala.
Police Officers' Association (KPOA) and the Kerala.
Police Senior Officers' Association (KPSOA).
Under the restructuring, the State had decided to abolish the KPOA and redistribute its members between the KPA and KPSOA.
The arrangement envisaged bringing Civil.
Police Officers, Senior Civil Police.

Officers, Grade Assistant Sub Inspectors, Assistant Sub Inspectors and Grade Sub Inspectors under the KPA, while directly recruited Sub Inspectors and officers in the regular promotional hierarchy, including Inspectors, Deputy Superintendents of Police and Superintendents of Police (Non-IPS), would be grouped under the KPSOA.

The associations challenged the government order before the Kerala High Court, arguing that the existing associations functioned under government-approved bylaws and their organisational structure could not be altered contrary to those rules.

stories.headline: Tamil Nadu Government Moves Supreme Court Challenging Madras HC Order To Remove Periyar Statue From Temple Land
stories.title: Tamil Nadu Government Moves Supreme Court Challenging Madras HC Order To Remove Periyar Statue From Temple Land
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Tamil Nadu Government has approached the Supreme Court challenging the Madras High Court's order directing the removal of a statue of Dravidian movement leader and reformer EV Ramasamy, popularly known as Periyar, installed near the Arulmigu Bramasirakandeeswarar Temple in Thanjavur district.

The Madras High Court, by its order dated October 30, 2026, had directed the Thanjavur District Collector to safely remove the statue from the temple land and relocate it to another suitable place within four weeks.
The Court had also directed the State authorities to file a compliance report and listed the matter after four weeks to verify compliance.

The Division Bench comprising Justices P Velmurugan and K Ramakrishnan passed the order while hearing a writ petition filed by Rama Ravikumar, a devotee, seeking the removal of the statue from the temple premises.

The petitioner had sought the removal of the statue in light of a recommendation made by the Joint Commissioner of the Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments (HR&CE) Department, Thanjavur, in proceedings dated July 8, 2026.
The petitioner had alleged that the statue was installed by the Dravidar Kazhagam in 1990 without obtaining the necessary permission from the HR&CE Department.
He had also objected to the inscription beneath the statue, which carries Periyar's statement denying the existence of God.

During the proceedings, the High Court had directed the District Collector to conduct a physical inspection of the location and ascertain whether the statue stood on temple land or government poramboke land.
The authorities subsequently informed the Court that the statue was situated on land belonging to the temple and not on government poramboke land.

Taking note of the status report submitted by the District Collector, the Bench observed that the statue had been installed on temple land without obtaining permission from the temple authorities, the District Collector or any other competent authority.
Accordingly, the Court directed the District Collector to remove the statue safely and relocate it to another suitable place within four weeks.
The Court disposed of the writ petition with the above directions and ordered the matter to be listed after four weeks for reporting compliance.
